newsitem.title: UK: Foreign investors stoke Russian equity stakes.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors stoke Russian equity stakes.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health problems are being shrugged off by foreign investors at the start of a year in which most are increasing holdings in a market that has become more accessible and more acceptable.
"Mainstream foreign fund managers have started to build substantial stakes in Russia for the first time," said Matt Linsey, emerging markets fund manager for the ING bank group in Luxembourg.

For those who invested in 1996, Russia was an exceptionally rewarding place to be. The CSFB ROS index of leading Russian shares has tripled in value from its March low of 522, while the price of Vneshekonombank debt rose two-and-a-half times.
On Thursday and Friday, Russian shares again roared ahead as investors ignored Yeltsin's health. The ROS index has risen to 1,656.50 points from 1,390.20 at the end of 1996.
Doctors said Yeltsin, in hospital with pneumonia, was breathing more easily but there had been no dramatic improvement in his condition.
"I have 10 percent of my fund in Russia at present and it is zero percent of my benchmark index. Russia has been a very good place to be for my investors in the past year," Linsey said.

All this happened in a year when a Communist-dominated parliament took office, a Communist presidency had been possible, bloodshed plagued Chechnya, Yeltsin had his heart operation, there was a tax collection crisis and the International Monetary Fund threatened to pull away its financial support.

In the coming year, a series of major deals for Russian companies will see energy, banking and manufacturing enterprises tap foreign capital markets and the "Holy Grail" of a full New York Stock Exchange listing will be achieved by others such as natural gas giant Gazprom.

Already, U.S. bank Chase Manhattan offers U.S. mutual funds custody in 700 Russian securities, while company accounts are improving and the International Finance Corporation will launch its Russia share index on February 1.

"It is very important that the Russian equity market is seen to behave like a normal market in which companies can raise money at reasonable prices," said Mark Cooke, fund manager at Brunswick Capital Management in London.
Others say the market and the Russian economy are now more important than politics.

"The decline of inflation and interest rates will prove more significant to the Russian renaissance in 1997-99 than whether Boris Yeltsin retains the presidency," said Daiwa Institute of Research chief equity strategist Roger Monson.

Yet the economic policies that called a halt to hyperinflation -- inflation slowed to an annual 24 percent in November 1996 from 131 percent in December 1995 -- might well expose some Russian companies.

"The main effect of high inflation over the past few years has been to exaggerate the profitability of enterprises by producing artificial profits on holding inventories and reducing the depreciation charge in real terms," said Morgan Stanley Russian equity analyst John-Paul Smith.
ING's Linsey says the strong start to 1997 makes him nervous and he wants to trim his exposure to Russia.
"Although I remain bullish on the longer term and will keep around seven percent of my fund in Russia, it is always worrying when you see a liquidity-driven market.

Brunswick's Cooke is less worried. "One is invevitably drawn to Russia unless valuations become outrageous. There are very few other places in the world where the sort of returns we are seeing there can be achieved," he said.
